source.title: Over-training with Mixup May Hurt Generalization

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results qualifying when Mixup helps generalization: it can improve early test performance, then worsen it with continued training; the effect varies with dataset size, augmentation, architecture, and mixing coefficient.
record.gate_note: The paper tests over-training with Mixup and related test-error dynamics. The random-label capacity results are cited prior work, not results from this study. Several results are figure-only, so precise values are not recoverable from the text.
record.test_reason: The study reports Mixup training dynamics, which none of V1–V8 names. Its loss-landscape visualizations do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Random-label fitting is cited prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report U-shaped Mixup generalization dynamics and attribute late deterioration to fitting data-dependent synthetic-label noise. They suggest that training dynamics and stopping criteria may matter more than fully optimizing the loss. Their regression analysis offers an explanation rather than establishing this mechanism universally for classification.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates extended Mixup training and Mixup-to-ERM switching, rather than the original claim's random-label memorization, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, size, or generalization-measure interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with training duration, dataset size, data augmentation, dataset, architecture, mixing coefficient, and switch time. For covariate-shift tests it varies by shift dataset/severity.

fits_no_version.finding: Extended Mixup training can worsen held-out performance; smaller datasets bring deterioration earlier, while augmentation delays it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixup can produce U-shaped test-error dynamics whose turning point depends on dataset size and augmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed-feature teacher–student regression exhibits U-shaped Mixup test loss, with deterioration occurring earlier as the mixing coefficient approaches 0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixup-induced noise can produce late deterioration in random-feature regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Appropriately timed switching from Mixup to ERM can avoid deterioration; switching too early or late is less beneficial.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The timing of a Mixup-to-ERM switch affects held-out performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixup gradient norms remain nonzero during training and rapidly approach zero after switching to ERM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixup can generalize well before reaching a stationary point.

fits_no_version.finding: Longer Mixup training reduces CIFAR10.1 and CIFAR10.2 accuracy but improves accuracy under severity-5 Gaussian corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixup over-training effects depend on the evaluation distribution and corruption severity.

fits_no_version.finding: RegMixup with η=2 behaves similarly to Mixup; η=0.1 delays deterioration without eliminating it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RegMixup's resistance to over-training depends on its mixing-loss weight.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report sharper empirical-risk landscape visualizations with longer Mixup training, alongside poorer standard-test accuracy but improved severe-corruption accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Qualitative landscape sharpness can accompany different test-performance trends depending on the evaluation distribution.

record.problems: Many results are presented only in figures without extractable exact values. Several experiments are described as single trials or do not state uncertainty in the main text. The toy regression setup is explicitly described as not perfectly explaining the classification behavior. The paper says data augmentation's effect is arguably mediated by increased training-set size, not independently isolated.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports a large number of additional architecture/dataset combinations, including ResNet34 and VGG16 on CIFAR10 and SVHN in Appendix B.1, MSE-loss experiments in Figure 13, further shifted evaluation for 30% CIFAR10 in Figure 16, and loss-landscape sharpness visualizations in Figures 2, 9, 15, and 16. They are not separately listed where they repeat the same qualitative Mixup over-training result across additional settings or show only figure-based trajectories; the sharpness comparisons do not provide extractable perturbation-tolerance measurements for V7.

untested.parts: No original experiment comparing fixed random-label fitting and held-out performance with natural-label training.
No width sweep beyond the width needed for zero training error; epoch-wise dynamics do not test width-wise generalization.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected image-classification comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-optimizer-versus-SGD comparison, optimizer tuning study, or Adam-to-SGD switch.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted large-batch recipes.
No dropout intervention or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.

No measurement of magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance against generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, or ranking comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Qualitative loss-landscape visualizations do not establish these quantities.
No influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples compared with equal-size random removals.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain outside the listed versions. Their cannot_determine states indicate that their measures cannot establish a listed effect, not that the reported Mixup findings are unreadable. The qualitative sharpness results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing results. V7 should be changed from tested_not_extracted to not_tested.

versions.untested_parts: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) but does not test random-label fitting or compare natural-label and random-label held-out performance.
No width sweep of one-hidden-layer ReLU networks across the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.

The study discusses loss-landscape sharpness alongside generalization, but reports these comparisons in figures without extractable numerical values or a text statement relating magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance to the generalization gap.
No removal of memorized examples or comparison with random-example removal.
